children: By José de Córdoba and James T. Areddy

The U.S. expelled a Cuban diplomat after the island country's foreign minister loudly interrupted an address by U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz criticizing Havana's leadership, and the two shouted at one another in an extraordinary exchange at the world body's famous rostrum.

The heated words and a battle over a cellphone unfolded Tuesday on the U.N. General Assembly floor during an annual debate about the U.S. economic embargo of Cuba, as Waltz laid out familiar American allegations that the Havana regime has enriched itself as it impoverished the population.

The now-departed Cuban official, Richard Tur de la Concepcion, is listed as the first secretary of the Cuban Mission and was involved in an altercation in the hall with another member of the U.S. delegation around the same time as the shouting. He was accused of hitting the American's cellphone as it was recording.

In a video Waltz posted online Tuesday, Tur de la Concepcion is seen smacking the cellphone recording him and saying, "he violated my personal space." In his post, Waltz said, one of the "regime's 'diplomats' tried to intimidate U.N. staff into cutting our microphones as I exposed the regime for the world to see."

A State Department spokesman said Wednesday, "We have made clear to the Cuba Mission that this individual is not welcome in the United States, and as a result this individual has left." The spokesman didn't provide details. Both the shouting and the cellphone episodes took place inside the U.N.'s famous General Assembly Hall but at different locations.

The incidents, together with the expulsion, illustrate the increasingly bitter tenor and deteriorating relations between the U.S. and its communist neighbor during the Trump administration. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Waltz periodically denounce the Cuban government. President Trump has implemented tough sanctions that have brought the island's already ailing economy to a halt and has repeatedly hinted at military intervention to overthrow the Cuban leadership.
The U.S. has a number of times in the past ordered Cuban diplomats out of the country but usually after accusations of spying.

Waltz had taken the U.N. podium Tuesday nearly an hour into an annual debate about the U.S. embargo of Cuba and immediately accused the late Cuban leader Fidel Castro of sending thousands to "concentration camps," prompting loud hackles from Cuba's delegation.

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez and his team of diplomats began pounding their desks, with one making a timeout motion and others demanding that the presiding official respect "procedural" rules that would allow them a response.

Rodríguez, followed by other Cuban diplomats, then walked toward the rostrum where Waltz was speaking to address the presider, Bangladesh's Khalilur Rahman who is president of the U.N. Security Council and was seated behind the U.S. ambassador.
As the Cubans requested time to speak, Waltz taunted them. "This is America, my friend," Waltz shouted, tapping his fingers for emphasis. "You cannot silence me," he said, adding, "Back up!"
Rodríguez didn't approach Waltz, nor did he appear to address the ambassador directly, even as both men continued to speak in loud voices.
After an exchange near the podium, Rodríguez returned to the Cuban delegation's seats and was given an opportunity to speak. He accused Waltz of "lying grossly."

Over the next half-hour or so, the Cuban delegation repeatedly shouted objections and pounded on their table as Waltz used photos of what he said were expensive watches and a private island to build a case that Castro, his family and other members of the Cuban elite lived lavish lifestyles, in contrast to the communist philosophies, that "would make New York socialites blush."

Cuba's ambassador to the U.N., Ernesto Soberon, on Wednesday issued an open letter to the U.N. secretary-general that accused a Waltz spokesman of harassing his colleague, Tur de la Concepcion, by violating his personal space in using a cellphone to take videos.
The letter made no mention of an expulsion, and the Cuban Consulate didn't respond to questions about it.
At the end of the proceedings, 130 U.N. members voted to support a resolution calling on the U.S. to end its trade embargo against Cuba, with 17 against it and 25 members abstaining.
